claims.text: The starting material is a conventionally cast, polycrystalline high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution and standard grain-boundary chemistry.
A small tungsten addition followed by annealing will selectively segregate tungsten to grain boundaries.
Tungsten segregation will alter the alloy's grain-boundary chemistry.
Tungsten segregation may produce thin, continuous intergranular phases.
Controlled annealing causes tungsten atoms to preferentially segregate to grain boundaries.
Segregated tungsten layers or tungsten-containing precipitates strengthen grain boundaries.
Strengthening the grain boundaries reduces grain-boundary sliding.
Reduced grain-boundary sliding improves resistance to high-temperature creep.
The tungsten-doped alloy will have a lower elevated-temperature creep rate than the undoped baseline.
The tungsten-doped alloy will have a higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the undoped baseline.
The predicted mechanical benefits should hold from approximately 800°C to 1000°C.
The benefit may disappear outside 800°C to 1000°C or under substantially different loading conditions.
A failure to obtain either a greater than 10% creep-rate reduction or a greater than 10% yield-strength increase is proposed as the falsification criterion.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome asserts both reduced creep rate and increased yield strength, while the 'and/or' falsification rule can treat improvement in only one endpoint as sufficient, leaving failure of the other asserted prediction non-falsifying.
